question: In which compilation are the devotional songs of the Alvar saints collected?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nalayira Divya Prabandham.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The hymns of the Vaishnava Alvar saints of Tamil country are gathered in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, meaning the 'four thousand divine verses' (आलवार संतों के भजनों का संकलन — नालायिर दिव्य प्रबंधम्)

 

• The Alvars were devotees of Vishnu, and tradition counts 12 of them, among them Periyalvar, Andal and Nammalvar.

 

• The collection was arranged in the 10th century by Nathamuni, and it became a sacred text for the Sri Vaishnava tradition that Ramanuja later systematised.

 

• The verses are in Tamil, which shows how Bhakti used the regional language instead of Sanskrit to reach ordinary devotees.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Andal is the only woman among the twelve Alvars; her Tiruppavai is still sung during the Margazhi month.

 

• The Shaiva counterparts of the Alvars were the 63 Nayanars, and their hymns form the Tirumurai.

 

• Early Bhakti in the Tamil country dates from roughly the 6th to 9th centuries and was patronised by Pallava and Chola rulers.

 

• The twelve Alvars came from different social backgrounds, and their Tamil poems on temple towns made Vaishnava devotion open to women and lower castes as well.

 

NOTE

 

• Tirumurai (Option 1): The Tirumurai is the Shaiva canon of Tamil hymns composed by the Nayanars, who worshipped Shiva, so it belongs to the rival devotional stream rather than to the Vishnu-worshipping Alvars.

 

• Adi Granth (Option 2): The Adi Granth is the Sikh scripture, compiled by Guru Arjan Dev in 1604 from the hymns of the early Gurus and some Bhakti saints, and it is entirely unconnected with the Alvars of South India.

 

• Gita Govinda (Option 4): The Gita Govinda is a Sanskrit lyrical poem of the 12th century by Jaidev of Bengal on the love of Radha and Krishna; it is a single poetic work, not a compilation of Alvar songs.

question: The Nayanar saints of the Tamil country were devotees of which deity?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shiva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Nayanars were Tamil saints who worshipped Shiva, and tradition counts 63 of them (तमिल नायनार संत शिव के उपासक थे)

 

• Their devotional poems were later collected in the Tirumurai, with the Tevaram of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar forming its most revered part.

 

• In the Bhakti tradition a worshipper of Shiva is called a Nayanar, while a worshipper of Vishnu is called an Alvar.

 

• The two streams together made up the early Bhakti movement of South India, which preached personal devotion to God in the language of the people.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar are the three best-known Nayanar poets.

 

• Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a woman Nayanar who composed Shaiva hymns.

 

• Chola kings such as Rajaraja I promoted the Shaiva hymns by installing them in temples.

 

• The Nayanar saints included people of several castes, and their pilgrimage songs on Shaiva temples such as Chidambaram and Madurai spread devotion to Shiva across the Tamil region.

 

NOTE

 

• Vishnu (Option 2): Vishnu was the god of the Alvars, the other great group of Tamil devotional poets; the Nayanars are specifically defined as Shaivites, so assigning them to Vishnu reverses the two traditions.

 

• Durga (Option 3): Durga is worshipped within the Shakta tradition and is not the focus of the Nayanar movement, whose sixty-three saints sang exclusively in praise of Shiva and his temples across Tamil Nadu.

 

• Surya (Option 4): Surya is the sun god of the Saura tradition, which was a minor sect, and the Nayanar saints of Tamil Nadu never centred their devotion on him but on Shiva.

question: The philosopher Ramanujacharya, who gave the doctrine of Vishishtadvaita, was born in which region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tamil Nadu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ramanuja was born in Tamil Nadu in about 1017 AD, in the 11th century, and he propounded Vishishtadvaita, or qualified monism (रामानुज का जन्म तमिलनाडु में 11वीं सदी में हुआ — विशिष्टाद्वैत)

 

• His philosophy challenged the strict Advaita of Shankara: for him God is Saguna Brahman, with attributes, and the soul and the world are real parts of God.

 

• He was deeply influenced by the Alvars, whose Tamil devotional hymns shaped his Sri Vaishnava thinking.

 

• He composed the Sri Bhashya, a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, to defend his view against the Advaitins.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Madhavacharya, born in the Kannada country, taught Dvaita or dualism.

 

• Shankara, who taught Advaita, came from Kerala and lived in the 8th century.

 

• Ramanuja's ideas on devotion to a personal God prepared the ground for later Bhakti saints like Ramananda.

 

• After Ramanuja, the Sri Vaishnava tradition split into later schools, and his teaching that all souls can reach God by bhakti and surrender (prapatti) appealed to many castes.

 

NOTE

 

• Karnataka (Option 1): Karnataka is the region of Madhavacharya, the dualist philosopher, and of the Veerashaiva movement, but Ramanuja himself was a Tamil Brahmin from near Madras, not a native of the Kannada country.

 

• Kerala (Option 3): Kerala is the birthplace of Adi Shankara, the exponent of Advaita, so the region is linked with the philosopher whom Ramanuja opposed rather than with Ramanuja's own origin.

 

• Andhra Pradesh (Option 4): Andhra Pradesh was not the birthplace of Ramanuja, although he later travelled widely; his early life and his tradition of Sri Vaishnavism are tied to the Tamil country and Srirangam.

question: Which of the following works was composed by Tulsidas in addition to the Ramcharitmanas?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kavitavali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tulsidas composed the Kavitavali and also the Gitavali, along with his masterpiece, the Ramcharitmanas (तुलसीदास की रचनाएँ — कवितावली व गीतावली)

 

• The Ramcharitmanas retells the Ramayana of Valmiki, which was in Sanskrit, in Awadhi, the Hindi dialect of the common people.

 

• Tulsidas was a worshipper of Lord Rama, so his work belongs to the Saguna stream of Bhakti.

 

• He is regarded as a contemporary of Akbar, and his Awadhi epic made the Rama story widely known in North India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vinay Patrika and Dohavali are two more known works by Tulsidas.

 

• Valmiki's Ramayana is the Sanskrit original that the Ramcharitmanas follows in story.

 

• The Ramcharitmanas was begun in Ayodhya in the 16th century, according to tradition.

 

• Tulsidas's Awadhi Ramcharitmanas is divided into seven kandas, like Valmiki's Ramayana, and it remains the most widely read version of the Rama story in North India.

 

NOTE

 

• Bijak (Option 1): The Bijak is the collection of poems and sayings of Kabir, the Nirguna saint of Banaras, and has no connection with the Rama-devotee Tulsidas, who worked in Awadhi.

 

• Sur Sagar (Option 2): Sur Sagar is the famous collection of Krishna lyrics by Surdas, who was a disciple of Vallabhacharya and popularised the Krishna cult in North India.

 

• Geet Govind (Option 3): Geet Govind was written in Sanskrit by Jaidev of Bengal in the 12th century on the theme of Radha and Krishna; it long predates Tulsidas and is not his work.

question: Surdas, the saint who popularised the Krishna cult in North India, was a disciple of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vallabhacharya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Surdas was a disciple of Vallabhacharya, the founder of the Pushtimarg, and he spread devotion to Krishna in North India (सूरदास वल्लभाचार्य के शिष्य थे — कृष्ण भक्ति)

 

• Vallabhacharya's philosophy was Shuddhadvaita, or pure non-dualism, and his path of grace was called Pushtimarg.

 

• The teaching was to devote oneself to Lord Krishna, who would then take the devotee to salvation.

 

• Surdas sang in Brij Bhasha, and his poems on the childhood of Krishna are collected in the Sur Sagar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vallabhacharya was from Andhra origin and settled at Mathura-Vrindavan region.

 

• The Pushtimarg tradition grew around the temple of Shrinathji at Nathdwara in Rajasthan.

 

• The Ashtachhap were eight poets of the Pushtimarg tradition, and Surdas was foremost among them.

 

• Surdas is traditionally described as blind, and his lyrics on the childhood pranks and youthful love of Krishna in Brij Bhasha remain staples of North Indian devotional music.

 

NOTE

 

• Ramanujacharya (Option 1): Ramanujacharya lived in the 11th-12th centuries and founded Vishishtadvaita in the Tamil country; he was long dead before Surdas and could not have been his teacher.

 

• Ramananda (Option 2): Ramananda belonged to the Rama tradition at Allahabad and Banaras and had disciples such as Kabir and Raidas; Surdas is associated with Krishna worship rather than with his school.

 

• Madhavacharya (Option 4): Madhavacharya taught Dvaita, or dualism, in the Kannada region around the 13th century; he is chronologically and doctrinally far from Surdas, a Krishna poet of the Pushtimarg.

question: Meera Bai, the Bhakti poetess devoted to Lord Krishna, belonged to which royal family and city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mewar - Chittor.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Meera Bai was a Rajput princess of Mewar, associated with the city of Chittor (मीराबाई मेवाड़ की राजकुमारी थीं — चित्तौड़)

 

• She composed lyrics in praise of Lord Krishna in the Brij Bhasha of Rajasthan, and her bhajans are popular in Rajasthan to this day.

 

• In the Saguna and Nirguna classification of the notes, she is listed with Tulsidas and Chaitanya as a Saguna devotee.

 

• Her intense devotion defied the conventions of her royal household, and she is a symbol of personal love for God.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tradition makes her the wife of Bhoj Raj, the son of Rana Sanga of Mewar.

 

• Her songs are often addressed to Giridhar Gopal, a name of Krishna.

 

• She is said to have spent her last years at Dwarka in Gujarat.

 

• Meera Bai's songs are addressed to Krishna as her beloved, and she is remembered for rejecting royal comforts and social convention in favour of personal devotion.

 

NOTE

 

• Marwar - Jodhpur (Option 1): Marwar and its capital Jodhpur were ruled by the Rathors, a different clan; Meera's early life is associated with the Rathor family of Merta, but her marriage and fame belong to Mewar.

 

• Amber - Jaipur (Option 2): Amber near Jaipur was the seat of the Kachhwaha clan; it is known for Raja Man Singh and Mughal alliances, and it has no link with the Mewar princess Meera Bai.

 

• Bundi - Kota (Option 3): Bundi and Kota belong to the Hada Chauhan region of south-east Rajasthan and are not the place of the princess who sang Krishna bhajans from Chittor.

question: Who among the following authored the 'Bijak', a collection of devotional poems and teachings?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kabir.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bijak is the collection of devotional poems and teachings attributed to Kabir (बीजक — कबीर की वाणी का संग्रह)

 

• Kabir was a Nirguna Bhakti saint who opposed idol worship, the supremacy of the Brahmin and the caste system.

 

• He stressed the oneness of all religions by describing Hindus and Muslims as pots of the same clay, and he lived in Banaras.

 

• His verses in simple spoken Hindi reached weavers, artisans and peasants, and later gave rise to the Kabir Panth.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kabir's dohas and sakhis are also preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib.

 

• Tradition makes him a disciple of Ramananda, though he preached a formless God.

 

• The Kabir Panth was formed by his followers after his death.

 

• Kabir's teaching combined elements of Hindu Bhakti and Sufi thought, and his followers came from both communities, with the Kabir Panth still active today.

 

NOTE

 

• Guru Nanak (Option 1): Guru Nanak founded the Sikh faith and his hymns, such as Japji, are in the Guru Granth Sahib; the Bijak is not his work, although he was a contemporary of Kabir in the Nirguna tradition.

 

• Raidas (Option 3): Raidas was a Nirguna saint, regarded as a disciple of Ramananda and a cobbler by caste, but the Bijak is the text of Kabir, not a book that Raidas compiled.

 

• Namdev (Option 4): Namdev was a Maharashtra saint associated with the Warkari tradition of Vithoba at Pandharpur, whose verses also appear in Sikh scripture, but he did not author the Bijak.

question: Which Bhakti saint was the first to use a regional language, Hindi, to spread Bhakti and established the Rama cult?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ramananda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ramananda, born at Allahabad, was the first Bhakti saint to use a regional language, Hindi, to spread devotion (रामानंद — हिंदी में भक्ति प्रचार करने वाले पहले संत)

 

• He worshipped Lord Ram and Sita and thus established the Rama cult in North India.

 

• He opposed the caste system and accepted disciples from every caste, a social message that became a mark of the Nirguna and Saguna saints alike.

 

• His disciples traditionally include Kabir, Raidas and Pipa, and the first two spread his message among the lower castes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ramananda is placed in the 14th-15th centuries and worked mainly at Banaras.

 

• His order became known as the Ramanandi sect, the largest group of Vaishnava ascetics in North India.

 

• Tulsidas's Rama devotion is part of the wider tradition that Ramananda promoted.

 

• Ramananda moved the centre of Bhakti from the South to Banaras in the north, which made it possible for a message born in the Tamil country to reach Hindi-speaking regions.

 

NOTE

 

• Kabir (Option 2): Kabir was a disciple in the Ramananda tradition and a Nirguna poet, but the credit of first using Hindi for Bhakti and founding the Rama cult is given to his teacher and not to him.

 

• Vallabhacharya (Option 3): Vallabhacharya founded the Pushtimarg centred on Lord Krishna, not Rama, and his philosophy was Shuddhadvaita; he is therefore not the saint who established the Rama cult.

 

• Chaitanya (Option 4): Chaitanya of Nadiya in Bengal considered himself an incarnation of Krishna and Radha, and he introduced sankirtan; his devotion was Krishna-centred, so the Rama cult is not his.

question: Who composed the 'Geet Govind', a work on Radha and Krishna, in the 12th century?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jaidev.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jaidev, the first noted devotional poet of Bengal, composed the Geet Govind in the 12th century (जयदेव — गीत गोविंद के रचयिता)

 

• The poem is about the love of Radha and Krishna, and its music is emotional and esoteric, which set the tone of Bengal's Bhakti.

 

• Bhakti in Bengal was different in spirit from that in North and South India, and was taken to its peak by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

 

• Jaidev is said to have lived at the court of Lakshmana Sena of Bengal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Geet Govind is composed in Sanskrit in twelve cantos.

 

• Its verses are still performed in the Jagannath temple at Puri.

 

• Vidyapati of Mithila later composed Radha-Krishna songs in Maithili.

 

• Jaidev's lyrics are also set to ragas and talas and were sung in temples, making the Geet Govind both a poem and a musical text of the Radha-Krishna tradition.

 

NOTE

 

• Chaitanya (Option 1): Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is the saint who took Bengal's Bhakti to its peak and popularised sankirtan; he did not compose the Geet Govind, which was already centuries old when he was born.

 

• Surdas (Option 2): Surdas was a Brij Bhasha poet and disciple of Vallabhacharya whose Krishna songs are in the Sur Sagar; he is from the Mathura-Agra region and lived much later than the 12th-century Geet Govind.

 

• Vidyapati (Option 3): Vidyapati composed love songs on Radha and Krishna in Maithili in the 14th-15th centuries, so he is a later poet in the same theme, but he is not the writer of Geet Govind.

question: The classical dance form Sattriya was introduced by which Bhakti saint of Assam, who propagated 'Eka Sarana Nama Dharma'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shankardeva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shankardeva of Assam, a saint, scholar and social reformer, promoted the devotional philosophy of Eka Sarana Nama Dharma and introduced the Sattriya dance (शंकरदेव — असम के संत; सत्रिया नृत्य, एक शरण नाम धर्म)

 

• The faith centres on devotion to one God, Krishna, through the chanting of his name, without elaborate rituals or caste distinctions.

 

• Sattriya developed in the monasteries called Sattras, set up by Shankardeva, and it is now counted among India's classical dances.

 

• His movement made Assam a major centre of Vaishnava Bhakti in the 15th-16th centuries.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sattriya was recognised as a classical dance by the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 2000.

 

• Shankardeva also composed Borgeets, devotional songs, and one-act plays called Ankiya Nat.

 

• His chief disciple Madhavdeva carried the movement forward.

 

• Shankardeva's Borgeets and the Kirtan Ghosha are the best known of his literary works, and his teaching spread widely among the peoples of the Brahmaputra valley.

 

NOTE

 

• Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (Option 2): Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was the saint of Bengal who popularised sankirtan, group devotional singing with dancing; he is linked with the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition and not with Assam's Sattriya.

 

• Namdev (Option 3): Namdev belonged to Maharashtra and the Varkari tradition of Vithoba, composing abhangs in Marathi; he has no link with the Sattras or the dance of Assam.

 

• Basavanna (Option 4): Basavanna was the 12th-century reformer of the Veerashaiva or Lingayat movement in Karnataka, which worshipped Shiva and rejected caste hierarchy; his tradition is entirely separate from Assam's Vaishnavism.

question: The Veerashaiva (Lingayat) movement began in which present-day state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Karnataka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Veerashaiva or Lingayat movement began in Karnataka in the mid-12th century (वीरशैव/लिंगायत आंदोलन — कर्नाटक में आरंभ)

 

• It was led by Basavanna, a minister at the court of the Kalachuri king Bijjala, and it centred on the worship of Shiva in the form of a linga worn on the body.

 

• The movement criticised Brahmanical ritual, caste hierarchy and temple worship, and it gave importance to the Vachanas, short prose verses in Kannada.

 

• Its followers are known as Lingayats, and they remain numerous in Karnataka today.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Allama Prabhu and Akka Mahadevi were other prominent Veerashaiva saints.

 

• Anubhava Mantapa at Basavakalyan was the assembly where saints discussed spiritual questions.

 

• The Vachanas are among the earliest works of Kannada prose-poetry.

 

• Basavanna's followers wore the linga in a small casket around the neck, a practice that marked the break from temple-centred worship and from the Brahmin priesthood.

 

NOTE

 

• Assam (Option 1): Assam is the home of Shankardeva's Eka Sarana Nama Dharma, a Vaishnava stream; the Shiva-centred Lingayat movement did not arise there.

 

• Bengal (Option 2): Bengal's Bhakti was led by Jaidev and Chaitanya in the Krishna tradition, with emotional music and sankirtan, so it is not the origin of the Shaiva reform of Basavanna.

 

• Maharashtra (Option 3): Maharashtra's Bhakti centred on the Varkari saints worshipping Vithoba at Pandharpur, including Dnyaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram, rather than on the Lingayat reform that began to the south in Karnataka.

question: In his Ain-i-Akbari, Abul Fazl listed how many Sufi silsilas?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 14.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abul Fazl in the Ain-i-Akbari lists 14 Sufi silsilas, of which four were important and powerful (अबुल फजल ने आइन-ए-अकबरी में 14 सिलसिले गिनाए)

 

• The four major orders in India were the Chishti, Suhrawardi, Naqshbandi and Qadiri (Qadariya) silsilas.

 

• A silsila is a chain of spiritual descent in which a pir passes his teaching to a chosen disciple, or khalifa.

 

• Sufism was a liberal reform movement within Islam that reached India from Persia, and it stressed love and devotion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Ain-i-Akbari is the third volume of the Akbarnama, the history of Akbar's reign.

 

• The Chishti order was brought to India by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, and its centre was Ajmer.

 

• Sufi khanqahs served as centres of teaching and charity.

 

• Among the four main orders, the Chishti silsila was most associated with the poor and with khanqahs near the common people, while the Suhrawardi order was close to the ruling class.

 

NOTE

 

• 4 (Option 1): Four is the number of the important and powerful silsilas, not the total counted in the Ain-i-Akbari; Abul Fazl's list is much longer than the four leading orders.

 

• 12 (Option 2): Twelve is the traditional number of Alvar saints in the Vaishnava Bhakti tradition and is not the number of Sufi silsilas that Abul Fazl listed in his work.

 

• 22 (Option 4): Twenty-two is the number of administrative branches called Manjis, created by Guru Amar Das in Sikhism, and is not connected with the count of Sufi orders in the Ain-i-Akbari.

question: The practice of visiting the tomb of a Sufi saint, such as the dargah at Ajmer, is called:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ziyarat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ziyarat is the pilgrimage to a Sufi saint's grave, as at the Ajmer Dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (ज़ियारत — सूफी संत की मजार पर जाना)

 

• Devotees of every faith visit such dargahs to seek blessings, which showed the syncretic character of the Sufi movement in India.

 

• The death anniversary of a saint is observed as an Urs according to the Islamic lunar calendar, and it is not a birth celebration.

 

• Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti established the Chishti order in India, and his dargah became a centre of pilgrimage.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mughal emperors such as Akbar visited the Ajmer dargah, and Akbar went there on foot on one occasion.

 

• Nizamuddin Auliya's dargah at Delhi is another important place of ziyarat.

 

• Qawwali singing is common at dargahs and has links with Chishti gatherings, called sama.

 

• Famous Sufi dargahs include those of Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi and Baba Farid at Pakpattan, and they draw pilgrims of all communities.

 

NOTE

 

• Sankirtan (Option 1): Sankirtan is the group devotional singing with dancing that Chaitanya introduced in Bengal, a Hindu Bhakti practice; it concerns hymns, not visits to a saint's tomb.

 

• Langar (Option 2): Langar is the community kitchen of the Sikh tradition, where all sit together and eat regardless of caste, so it belongs to Sikhism and not to Sufi tomb visits.

 

• Wahdat-ul-wajud (Option 3): Wahdat-ul-wajud is the Sufi doctrine of the unity of being, which holds that God and creation are one; it is a philosophy, whereas the term asked about refers to a ritual visit.

question: Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, was born in 1469 at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Talwandi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Guru Nanak was born at Talwandi, near Lahore, in 1469, and now the place is called Nankana Sahib (गुरु नानक का जन्म तलवंडी में हुआ — 1469)

 

• He founded the Sikh religion, emphasised the worship of one God, and established the Nanak Panth.

 

• He was a contemporary of Kabir, and like Kabir he followed the Nirguna path with no Brahmin supremacy and no casteism.

 

• He named Guru Angad as his successor and died at Kartarpur in 1539.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word Sikh means disciple.

 

• Nankana Sahib is now in Pakistan's Punjab province.

 

• His hymns such as Japji Sahib are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

 

• Nanak travelled widely on journeys called Udasis and taught the message of Ik Onkar, meaning that God is one, in simple verses sung with the rabab played by Mardana.

 

NOTE

 

• Kartarpur (Option 2): Kartarpur is the town on the Ravi where Guru Nanak spent his last years and died in 1539, so it marks his death rather than his birth.

 

• Anandpur (Option 3): Anandpur is linked with Guru Teg Bahadur and Guru Gobind Singh, who later made it the centre from which the Khalsa was organised; it came into the story long after Nanak.

 

• Amritsar (Option 4): Amritsar was founded by Guru Ramdas, the fourth Guru, and has the Golden Temple; it did not exist as a city in the lifetime of the first Guru.

question: Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru, was originally known by which name?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lehna.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The original name of the second Guru, Guru Angad, was Lehna (गुरु अंगद का मूल नाम लहना)

 

• Guru Nanak chose him as his successor in preference to his own sons.

 

• To safeguard the purity of the Punjabi language, he created the Gurmukhi script, which is used to write the Sikh scriptures.

 

• His succession by merit, not by birth, set the pattern for the next Guru, since Nanak passed over his own sons.

 

• Lehna had earlier been a devotee of the goddess and led pilgrim parties, but he became a disciple of Nanak at Kartarpur and so impressed the founder that he was chosen over the Guru's sons.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gurmukhi literally means 'from the mouth of the Guru'.

 

• Guru Angad's hymns are included in the Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan.

 

• He is said to have promoted physical training with wrestling grounds called akharas.

 

• Guru Angad's name means 'part of the body', for Nanak accepted him almost as his own limb, and the Gurmukhi letters made the Punjabi hymns easy to read and copy.

 

NOTE

 

• Amar (Option 1): Amar was the earlier name of Guru Amar Das, who became the third Guru; he joined Guru Angad as a disciple and later succeeded him, so the name is not that of the second Guru.

 

• Ram Das (Option 2): Ram Das was the name taken by the fourth Guru, whose earlier name was Jetha; he founded Ramdaspur or Amritsar and was the son-in-law of Guru Amar Das.

 

• Jetha (Option 3): Jetha was the name of the youth who became Guru Ramdas, the fourth Guru, after marrying the daughter of Amar Das; it does not refer to the second Guru Angad.

question: Which Sikh Guru divided his spiritual empire into 22 parts known as Manjis?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guru Amar Das.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, divided his spiritual empire into 22 parts called Manjis for the propagation of Sikh ideas (गुरु अमरदास — 22 मंजी प्रणाली)

 

• Each Manji was in the charge of a devoted Sikh, so the system gave the early Sikh community an organised structure.

 

• The Mughal emperor Akbar visited him, and his daughter was married to the fourth Guru, Ramdas.

 

• These steps prepared the community for the larger institutions of later Gurus, such as the Adi Granth and the Akal Takht.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Guru Amar Das is also associated with strengthening the langar, where visitors ate together.

 

• He discouraged practices like sati and purdah among Sikhs, according to Sikh tradition.

 

• Goindwal became the centre of Sikh activity under him.

 

• The Manji network linked the scattered Sikh congregations of Punjab, and later a second kind of unit, called the Masand, collected offerings under the fourth and fifth Gurus.

 

NOTE

 

• Guru Angad (Option 2): Guru Angad devised Gurmukhi and gave attention to the Punjabi language; he is not credited with dividing the Sikh community into Manjis, which came a generation later.

 

• Guru Arjan Dev (Option 3): Guru Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth in 1604 and completed the Golden Temple; the Manji organisation had been set up by his maternal grandfather, the third Guru, well before.

 

• Guru Hargobind (Option 4): Guru Hargobind turned the Sikhs into a martial community and started the Akal Takht, so his contribution was military and political, not the 22-part system of preaching centres.

question: Which Sikh Guru founded the city of Amritsar, whose old name was Ramdaspur?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guru Ramdas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Guru Ramdas, the fourth Guru, founded the city of Amritsar, formerly named Ramdaspur (गुरु रामदास — अमृतसर/रामदासपुर के संस्थापक)

 

• He also began the construction of the Harmandir, the Golden Temple, in the city.

 

• The land for the temple is traditionally said to have been given by Akbar.

 

• The temple was completed by his son and successor, Guru Arjan Dev, who made Amritsar the centre of Sikhism.

 

• The tank dug at the site and the nearby settlement drew merchants and pilgrims, so Ramdaspur grew as a trading centre, which strengthened the Sikh community economically and made it easier to raise offerings.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Guru Ramdas was the son-in-law of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru.

 

• The Golden Temple has doors on all four sides, symbolising openness to every faith.

 

• The sacred tank around the shrine, the Amrit Sarovar, gave the city its name.

 

• Amritsar's name comes from the pool of nectar, the Amrit Sarovar, dug around the site, and the town grew into a trading and pilgrimage centre under the later Gurus.

 

NOTE

 

• Guru Arjan Dev (Option 1): Guru Arjan Dev completed the construction of the Golden Temple and compiled the Adi Granth, but the founding of the city under its older name was done by his father.

 

• Guru Hargobind (Option 2): Guru Hargobind fortified Amritsar and set up the Akal Takht there, so he strengthened the city rather than founding it.

 

• Guru Har Rai (Option 4): Guru Har Rai is known for a free Ayurvedic hospital and herbal garden, a humane work that is unrelated to the foundation of Amritsar.

question: Which Sikh Guru established the Akal Takht and took the title 'Padshah'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guru Hargobind.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, transformed the Sikhs into a martial community, started the Akal Takht, and took the title Padshah (गुरु हरगोबिंद — अकाल तख्त, पादशाह की उपाधि)

 

• He also fortified Amritsar, showing the shift from a purely spiritual movement to one ready for armed defence.

 

• The change followed the execution of his father, Guru Arjan Dev, by Jahangir.

 

• The Akal Takht stands opposite the Golden Temple and symbolises temporal authority alongside the spiritual authority of the Harmandir.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tradition says he wore two swords, symbolising miri (temporal) and piri (spiritual) power.

 

• He was imprisoned for some time at Gwalior fort under Jahangir.

 

• His militarisation was later carried forward by Guru Gobind Singh.

 

• The Akal Takht, meaning the throne of the Timeless One, remains the highest seat of Sikh religious authority, and decisions called hukamnamas are issued from it.

 

NOTE

 

• Guru Arjan Dev (Option 2): Guru Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth and was put to death by Jahangir for helping Khusrau; he followed the peaceful path and did not take the title Padshah or build the Akal Takht.

 

• Guru Teg Bahadur (Option 3): Guru Teg Bahadur, the ninth Guru, was executed by Aurangzeb after refusing to accept Islam, and his period was marked by sacrifice rather than the setting up of the Akal Takht.

 

• Guru Har Krishan (Option 4): Guru Har Krishan became Guru at the age of five and died young; his short term was too brief to create institutions like the Akal Takht.

question: Who was the youngest Sikh Guru, becoming Guru at the age of five years?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guru Har Krishan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, was the youngest Guru, who took the seat at the age of 5 years (गुरु हर कृष्ण — सबसे कम उम्र के गुरु)

 

• He was preceded by Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, who set up a free Ayurvedic hospital and herbal garden.

 

• He was followed by Guru Teg Bahadur, the ninth Guru, who was killed by Aurangzeb.

 

• His name is thus placed between the two Gurus noted for medical charity and martyrdom in the sequence of ten Gurus.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Guru Har Krishan died of smallpox in Delhi in 1664.

 

• Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi commemorates him.

 

• Guru Gobind Singh was nine years old when he became the tenth Guru.

 

• Guru Har Krishan's short tenure ended in 1664, and tradition says that he named his successor with the words 'Baba Bakale', pointing to Guru Teg Bahadur at Bakala.

 

NOTE

 

• Guru Har Rai (Option 1): Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, led the Sikhs as an adult; he is remembered for medical charity, not for being a child Guru.

 

• Guru Gobind Singh (Option 3): Guru Gobind Singh succeeded his father at the age of nine after the execution of Teg Bahadur; he was young, but he was not as young as the eighth Guru.

 

• Guru Hargobind (Option 4): Guru Hargobind became Guru after the death of Guru Arjan Dev when he was about eleven, so he was also a young Guru but older than the eighth.

question: Banda Bahadur, who led the Sikh rebellion against the Mughals after Guru Gobind Singh, was executed in Delhi in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1716.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Banda Bahadur was executed in Delhi in 1716 on the orders of Emperor Farrukhsiyar for refusing to convert to Islam (बंदा बहादुर — 1716 में फर्रुखसियर के आदेश पर दिल्ली में मृत्युदंड)

 

• He led a massive armed rebellion against the oppressive Mughal Empire right after the death of Guru Gobind Singh in 1708.

 

• Before his death, Gobind Singh had declared that the next Guru would be the Guru Granth Sahib, ending the line of personal Gurus.

 

• Banda's campaigns in Punjab are remembered as the first major Sikh attempt at political rule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Banda Bahadur was earlier an ascetic named Lakshman Das, whom Guru Gobind Singh met at Nanded.

 

• He fought the battle of Sirhind in 1710 and defeated the Mughal governor Wazir Khan.

 

• He established a capital at Lohgarh in the Himalayan foothills.

 

• After his capture, Banda Bahadur was taken in procession to Delhi in 1715-16, and his execution marked the end of the first phase of independent Sikh armed rule in Punjab.

 

NOTE

 

• 1708 (Option 1): Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708 at Nanded; it was after this date that the rebellion started, so the year marks the Guru's death, not the execution of Banda Bahadur.

 

• 1675 (Option 2): Guru Teg Bahadur was executed by Aurangzeb in 1675 at Delhi; that is about forty years before Banda's execution and was a separate event in Sikh history.

 

• 1699 (Option 4): The year 1699 is the founding of the Khalsa Panth at Baisakhi by Guru Gobind Singh, which came earlier than Banda's rebellion by many years.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Sufi movement in India:

1. Sufism was a liberal reform movement of Islam that came into India from Persia.

2. Sufis believed in Wahdat-ul-wajud, the unity of being.

3. The Naqshbandi, Qadiri and Chishti orders were all outside the list of the four important silsilas.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Sufism was a liberal reform movement of Islam, which originated in Persia and spread into India from about the 11th century (सूफी आंदोलन — इस्लाम का उदार सुधार आंदोलन, फारस से भारत)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Sufis held the doctrine of Wahdat-ul-wajud, the unity of being, which means that God and the creature are essentially the same.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: according to Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari, of the 14 silsilas, four were important and powerful, and these are the Chishti, Suhrawardi, Naqshbandi and Qadiri orders.

 

• Hence only the first two statements hold, and the third wrongly removes major orders from the principal list.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Chishti order was founded in India by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer.

 

• The Suhrawardi order was strong in Multan and Sindh, and it accepted royal patronage.

 

• Wahdat-ul-wajud is associated with the thought of Ibn Arabi.

 

• Moinuddin Chishti is believed to have arrived in India in the late 12th century and to have settled at Ajmer, where Akbar later made regular pilgrimages.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Adding statement 3 makes this pair wrong, because the Naqshbandi and Chishti orders are the very silsilas named among the four important ones, so statement 3 cannot be accepted along with statement 1.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): This choice keeps statement 3 and drops the true statement on Wahdat-ul-wajud; but the unity of being is a recognised Sufi belief, and the claim about silsilas is the one that fails.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Including statement 3 spoils this combination, since the four important orders in the Ain-i-Akbari include the Chishti, Suhrawardi, Naqshbandi and Qadiri silsilas, which are not excluded from the list.

question:
Consider the following statements about Kabir:

1. He was a Nirguna Bhakti saint.

2. He supported idol worship and the supremacy of the Brahmin.

3. He described Hindus and Muslims as pots of the same clay.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Kabir was a Nirguna Bhakti saint who worshipped a formless God, and his verses are collected in the Bijak (कबीर — निर्गुण भक्ति संत)

 

• Statement 2 is incorrect: Kabir was against idol worship, against the supremacy of the Brahmin and against the caste system, so he is a leading voice of Nirguna dissent.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: he stressed the oneness of religions by describing Hindus and Muslims as pots of the same clay.

 

• Kabir lived at Banaras, and the notes list him with Raidas, Guru Nanak and Pipa among Nirguna saints, most of whom came from the lower castes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tradition makes Kabir a weaver by occupation, living in Banaras.

 

• His verses are written in a mixed spoken language known as Sadhukkadi.

 

• Some of his dohas were included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

 

• Kabir lived in Banaras, the centre of orthodox Hinduism, and his sharp criticism of rituals made him as controversial as he was popular among weavers and the poor.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Statement 2 is false, so the pair that includes it cannot be right; Kabir attacked idol worship and Brahmin supremacy, and he did not support them.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Pairing statement 2 with statement 3 fails because statement 2 is untrue; Kabir rejected temple idols and priestly authority, though he did describe Hindus and Muslims as pots of the same clay.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Endorsing every statement here would treat the false statement about idol worship as correct, which would turn a Nirguna saint into a Saguna one, so this cannot be accepted.

question:
Consider the following statements about Chaitanya Mahaprabhu:

1. He was born in the Nadiya region of Bengal.

2. He was a Nirguna saint who opposed idol worship.

3. He introduced sankirtan, a form of group devotional singing with dancing.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was born in the Nadiya region of Bengal, where he took Bhakti to its peak (चैतन्य महाप्रभु — नदिया, बंगाल)

 

• Statement 2 is incorrect: he was a Saguna saint and so believed in idol worship, and he regarded himself as an incarnation of Krishna and Radha.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: sankirtan was introduced by him, a set of devotional songs accompanied by dancing.

 

• He did not accept the supremacy of the Brahmin, and he had both Hindu and Muslim disciples.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chaitanya's followers are known as Gaudiya Vaishnavas.

 

• He later settled at Puri in Odisha, where he spent his last years.

 

• Jaidev's Geet Govind had earlier shaped the Radha-Krishna devotion of Bengal.

 

• Chaitanya's mission centred on the repetition of the names of Krishna, and he is regarded by his followers as the combined form of Radha and Krishna.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 2): Statement 2 is wrong because Chaitanya was a Saguna devotee of Krishna who believed in idol worship, so any answer that includes it fails even though statement 1 on his birth is true.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Combining statements 2 and 3 fails since the Nirguna label does not suit a Krishna-worshipping saint who sang before images, though sankirtan is rightly credited to him.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three treats the claim of Nirguna belief as true, which contradicts his view of himself as an incarnation of Krishna and Radha and his temple-centred devotion.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Saguna and Nirguna traditions in medieval India:

1. Nirguna saints were against idol worship and Brahmin supremacy.

2. Meera Bai, Tulsidas and Chaitanya are counted among Saguna saints.

3. Kabir, Raidas, Guru Nanak and Pipa are counted among Saguna saints.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Nirguna saints rejected idol worship and Brahmin supremacy, and most of them came from the lower castes (निर्गुण — मूर्ति पूजा व ब्राह्मण वर्चस्व के विरोधी)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Meera Bai, Tulsidas and Chaitanya are Saguna devotees who worshipped a God with form, such as Krishna or Rama.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: Kabir, Raidas, Guru Nanak and Pipa are listed as Nirguna saints, and not as Saguna ones.

 

• The Saguna tradition tended to keep the caste order with Brahmin importance, while Nirguna saints challenged it directly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Saguna means God with attributes, while Nirguna means God without attributes.

 

• Shankara's Advaita is associated with Nirguna Brahman and Ramanuja's thought with Saguna Brahman.

 

• Surdas is another Saguna poet, devoted to Krishna.

 

• The distinction between Saguna and Nirguna reflects two attitudes to the divine, one personal and image-based, the other abstract, and the two streams sometimes mixed in the same poet.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Statements 2 and 3 cannot go together because statement 3 puts Kabir and Guru Nanak into the Saguna group, though they preached a formless God and rejected idol worship.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Joining statements 1 and 3 accepts the wrong placement of Kabir, Raidas, Nanak and Pipa; these four are Nirguna saints, so statement 3 is false.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Choosing the full set of statements wrongly accepts the mistaken statement 3; the Nirguna group of Kabir, Raidas, Guru Nanak and Pipa is not Saguna, so all three cannot be correct.

question:
Consider the following statements about Guru Arjan Dev:

1. He compiled the hymns of the four earlier Gurus along with his own into the Adi Granth in 1604.

2. He completed the construction of the Golden Temple at Amritsar.

3. He was put to death by Aurangzeb for refusing to accept Islam.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, compiled the compositions of Nanak, Angad, Amar Das and Ram Das with his own into the Adi Granth in 1604 (गुरु अर्जन देव — आदि ग्रंथ, 1604)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: he completed the construction of the Golden Temple, which had been started by Guru Ramdas.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: Arjan Dev helped Khusrau, the son of Jahangir, in his revolt, and he was then killed by Jahangir, not by Aurangzeb.

 

• The person executed by Aurangzeb for refusing conversion was the ninth Guru, Teg Bahadur.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Guru Arjan's martyrdom in 1606 led to the militarisation of the Sikhs under his son Hargobind.

 

• The Adi Granth was first installed at the Harmandir Sahib.

 

• Guru Gobind Singh later added the hymns of Guru Teg Bahadur to the scripture.

 

• The Adi Granth was first installed at the Harmandir Sahib in 1604, with Baba Buddha as its first granthi, and the Golden Temple was given four doors for all castes and creeds.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Statement 3 spoils this pair; Aurangzeb is linked with the execution of the ninth Guru Teg Bahadur, while Arjan Dev was killed in Jahangir's reign after supporting Prince Khusrau.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 3): Statements 1 and 3 fail together because the second statement on the Golden Temple is true but left out, and statement 3 names the wrong emperor for Arjan Dev's death.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Selecting all of them names Aurangzeb as the emperor who put Arjan Dev to death, whereas that Guru lived under Akbar and Jahangir, a long time before Aurangzeb's rule.
